questions.title: Are signatures required on financing company’s certification notices under Louisiana’s insurance‑premium finance statute?
questions.question_body:
In Williams v.
GoAuto
the opinion discusses La Rev Stat §9 3550(G)(3)(a), which says a finance company "must certify" certain facts before requesting cancellation.
Plaintiffs argue that the certificate lacks any signed name until after policy cancellation has already been effected.
The court rejects this claim because "certifying" does not explicitly invoke signing.
However I’m uncertain whether “certify” legally requires a bona fide signature or merely states facts
(either spoken or written)
whether electronic mails count.
Is there precedent in Louisiana case law interpreting “certify”
to mean "sign"?
How do courts view an attachment stamped by an employee after automatic cancellation?

questions.title:
"Receipt" versus "delivery":
Does an e‑mail satisfy Louisiana’s statutory receiving requirement?
questions.question_body:
"Receipt" is defined broadly in Black’s Law Dictionary,
and La Rev Stat §9 3550(G)(3)(b)(i) demands insurers consider cancellation requested once “receipt” of notice and statement.
In Williams v.
GoAuto
APAC emails GoAuto’s computer service at midnight, which then cancels enforcement.
Only afterward does an APAC employee stamp a hard copy.
Plaintiffs claim this means GoAuto never "received" notice so it could not cancel.
Does electronic mail qualify as providing "receipt," especially when handled solely within corporate systems?
How do courts distinguish physical possession from electronic reception?
